screens.title: Database Migration Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Database migrations are one of the riskiest parts of cloud moves because databases contain application state and business records. In this lesson you will learn how to choose a migration approach based on whether engines match, how to use AWS Database Migration Service for continuous replication, and when to apply the Schema Conversion Tool or Babelfish to reduce application changes. We will emphasize practical, low-downtime patterns: full initial load plus change data capture, staged cutover steps, and how to validate consistency before switching clients. A short example demonstrates creating DMS endpoints and a replication task from a source database to an Aurora PostgreSQL target. Finally, we will surface common mistakes—type mismatches, incomplete schema conversion, sizing and network issues—and how to mitigate them with testing and monitoring. By the end you will be able to describe a migration plan that balances risk, cost, and business constraints and pick the right AWS tools for homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations.

screens.title: Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous Migrations
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the two primary migration categories and why the distinction drives your plan. A homogeneous migration is when the source and target database engines are the same, for example Oracle to Oracle on RDS. The main complexity there is moving large volumes of data while minimizing downtime; most schema and code constructs remain compatible so the conversion effort is low. A heterogeneous migration is when engines differ, such as S Q L Server to Aurora PostgreSQL. Here the complexity rises because you must translate schemas, stored procedures, and sometimes application S Q L. Converting types, functions, and procedural code is often the most time-consuming work. A concrete example: moving a 500-gigabyte S Q L Server database with many T-S Q L stored procedures to Aurora PostgreSQL will likely require schema conversion, function rewrites, and compatibility testing. A common misconception is that DMS alone solves all heterogeneous issues; in fact DMS handles data movement but not full schema and procedural conversion. Key takeaway: identify the category early to allocate time and tools — native backups or replication for homogeneous moves, plus Schema Conversion Tool and manual refactor work for heterogeneous migrations. What migration type fits your project constraints and resourcing?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous
Definitions
Homogeneous Migration
Same engine on source and target; primary focus is data movement and minimizing downtime.
Heterogeneous Migration
Different engines; requires schema conversion, code refactor, and compatibility testing.
Common Misconception
Assuming DMS converts stored procedures. DMS migrates data; SCT handles schema and code analysis and conversion.
Key Takeaway

Classify the migration early to pick the right tools and estimate manual conversion effort.

Concrete Example
Scenario: A 500 GB SQL Server application with many stored procedures needs to move to Aurora PostgreSQL. This is a heterogeneous migration that requires SCT to detect incompatible stored procedures, manual refactoring of T-SQL to PL/pgSQL where needed, and DMS to migrate data with CDC to keep downtime short.
Check Your Understanding
  • Which migration type needs schema conversion?
  • Does DMS convert stored procedures automatically?

screens.title: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Database Migration Service is a managed service that moves data between heterogeneous and homogeneous engines while supporting ongoing replication. At its core DMS uses a replication instance — compute that reads changes from the source and applies them to the target. You configure a source endpoint and a target endpoint, then create a replication task that runs a migration type: full load, CDC, or full-load-and-CDC. The full-load-and-CDC pattern is critical for minimal downtime: DMS performs an initial complete copy and then streams ongoing changes so the target remains synchronized. A concrete example: create a replication instance sized by your workload and start a task that performs full load then CDC. Monitor replication lag, C P U, memory, and input and output; under-sizing the instance leads to lag and delayed cutover. A common misconception is to treat DMS as a one-time copy tool; instead it is intended for continuous replication and supports retries, transformation rules, and table mappings. Key takeaway: use DMS for controlled, monitored data movement and plan replication-instance sizing and network bandwidth to avoid replication bottlenecks. AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) means dms performs the data movement and continuous replication that enables near-zero downtime migrations when combined with proper sizing and monitoring.. In practical terms, what dms does and why it is central to minimal-downtime migrations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › AWS DMS
What DMS provides
  • Replication instance: the compute that performs migration tasks.
  • Endpoints: credentials and connection details for source and target.
  • Replication tasks: define table mappings and migration type (full load, CDC, or both).
  • Monitoring: metrics for lag, CPU, memory, and I/O to validate performance.
Common Mistake

Under-sizing the replication instance or ignoring network bandwidth produces replication lag and jeopardizes cutover windows.

Concrete scenario
You create a replication instance, configure an on-premises source endpoint and an Aurora PostgreSQL target endpoint, then start a task using full-load-and-CDC. Monitor replication lag in CloudWatch and the DMS console. Increase instance class if lag grows during peak times. Validate data with row counts and checksums before cutover.
Key Takeaway

DMS is for data movement plus CDC; size resources and network capacity to meet recovery-time objectives.

screens.title: DMS Migration Types and Task Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding migration types in DMS determines how you achieve your downtime goals. Full load copies existing data from source to target. Change Data Capture captures ongoing changes so you can keep source and target synchronized after the initial copy. The combination full-load-and-CDC is the go-to pattern for minimal downtime: DMS performs an initial full transfer and then streams changes until you are ready to cut over. A concrete example: for a 2 TB database with tight RTO constraints, run full load during an off-peak window, let CDC replicate transactional changes, and plan a short write freeze and verification window before flipping connections. Common misconception: choosing CDC only for an initial migration; CDC-only assumes the target already contains full data. Another operational detail is table mappings and transformation rules — decide which schemas and objects to include to reduce initial load size and speed validation. Key takeaway: pick full-load-and-CDC for minimal downtime and plan table selection, monitoring, and a verification strategy before the cutover. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › DMS Migration Types
Migration types
Full Load
Copies all current data; simplest but requires downtime if no CDC.
CDC (Change Data Capture)
Streams ongoing changes; used to keep target synchronized after initial load.
Full-load-and-CDC
Initial full copy plus CDC for minimal-downtime cutovers.
Operational checklist
  • Choose tables and schemas to include to limit data size.
  • Start full load during off-peak or in parallel with replication.
  • Monitor replication lag, transaction log retention, and network throughput.
  • Plan a short write freeze for cutover: stop writes, wait for catch-up, validate, and redirect clients.
Key Takeaway

Full-load-and-CDC is typically required when downtime must be minimal. Prepare table mappings and monitoring in advance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › DMS CLI Walkthrough
Terminal-style code panel
# Example conceptual commands for DMS setup
# 1. Create source endpoint
aws dms create-endpoint \
  --endpoint-identifier "onprem-oracle-source" \
  --endpoint-type "source" \
  --engine-name "oracle" \
  --username "dmsuser" \
  --password "yourpassword" \
  --server-name "onprem.database.com" \
  --port 1521

# 2. Create target endpoint
aws dms create-endpoint \
  --endpoint-identifier "aurora-pg-target" \
  --endpoint-type "target" \
  --engine-name "aurora-postgresql" \
  --username "pguser" \
  --password "yourpassword" \
  --server-name "aurora-pg-instance.example.rds.amazonaws.com" \
  --port 5432

# 3. Create replication instance
aws dms create-replication-instance \
  --replication-instance-identifier "dms-repl-instance" \
  --replication-instance-class "dms.t3.medium" \
  --allocated-storage 50

# 4. Create replication task (full-load-and-cdc)
aws dms create-replication-task \
  --replication-task-identifier "oracle-to-aurora-task" \
  --migration-type "full-load-and-cdc" \
  --table-mappings "file://table-mappings.json"
Annotations & Notes
  • Replace placeholders with your ARNs, security group IDs, and subnet group names.
  • Use table-mappings to include or exclude schemas and speed the initial load.
  • For on-premises sources, ensure connectivity and transaction log retention for CDC.
  • After creation, check the replication task state and CloudWatch metrics to monitor lag.
Key Takeaway

Script DMS setup for repeatability, but always validate with sampling and full verification before cutover.

screens.title: Continuous Replication and Cutover Steps
screens.narratorSegment: A predictable cutover reduces risk. Use these steps to move an application with minimal downtime. Phase one is full load: start DMS full-load to copy existing data. Phase two is CDC: enable continuous replication so changes on the source are applied to the target. Phase three is pre-cutover verification: run row-count and checksum comparisons on sample tables, run application smoke tests against the target in read-only mode if possible, and monitor replication lag until it is negligible. Phase four is the short write freeze: stop writes to the source database, let DMS apply outstanding changes, and verify there are no pending transactions. Phase five is the switch: update application connection strings to the new target and start the application. Phase six is post-cutover monitoring: ensure error logs and performance metrics are healthy and roll back if serious issues appear. A common misconception is skipping verification or trusting row counts alone; include functional smoke tests and data integrity checks. The key takeaway is to script verification and rollback procedures so the cutover is repeatable and testable in staging before production. Continuous Replication and Cutover Steps means full load, cdc, verification, write freeze, switch, and post-cutover monitoring form a repeatable path to minimal downtime.. In practical terms, a practical checklist for minimizing downtime and ensuring consistency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Cutover Steps
Cutover process — numbered checklist
  1. Full load: run initial DMS copy for selected tables and schemas.
  2. Enable CDC: start streaming ongoing changes to the target.
  3. Pre-cutover verification: run row counts, checksums, and smoke tests against target.
  4. Write freeze: stop writes to source, wait for CDC to apply remaining changes.
  5. Switch connections: update application endpoints and start services on the target.
  6. Monitor & validate: ensure logs, performance, and integrity are correct.
Verification
Use sample checksums, not only row counts, and include application smoke tests.
Rollback plan
Prepare an explicit rollback path and test it in staging so you can revert quickly if needed.
Monitoring
Watch replication lag, database errors, and application logs immediately after cutover.

screens.title: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)
screens.narratorSegment: The AWS Schema Conversion Tool analyzes a source database schema and application code that interacts with the database, producing an assessment of what can be automatically converted and what needs manual work. SCT scans tables, data types, stored procedures, functions, and triggers, then reports compatibility issues and provides converted schema artifacts when possible. A concrete scenario: migrating Oracle schemas to Aurora PostgreSQL, SCT may automatically convert many table definitions but flag complex PL/S Q L procedures for manual rewriting. A common misconception is expecting SCT to perform a flawless automatic conversion for all procedural code. In practice SCT reduces bulk manual work but you must review its recommendations and refactor complex logic. Practical steps include exporting SCT assessment reports, prioritizing high-risk stored procedures for manual conversion, and running iterative tests. Key takeaway: use SCT early to scope conversion effort and plan manual refactors, and integrate SCT findings into your migration timeline to avoid surprises during cutover. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common Migration Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: This screen lists common mistakes teams make during migration and how to avoid them. First, incomplete schema conversion happens when teams assume automated tools fix everything; SCT will flag incompatibilities but manual refactor for stored procedures and proprietary functions is often required. Second, data type mismatches can silently corrupt data if types are mapped incorrectly; always test edge cases and validate conversion logic. Third, network latency between source, replication instance, and target can slow replication and increase lag; for large migrations consider Direct Connect or replication instances in the same region and subnet placement. Fourth, under-sizing the replication instance leads to C P U or input and output bottlenecks and replication lag; monitor metrics and scale instances proactively. Fifth, transaction log retention must be configured so CDC can read changes; short retention causes missed changes. Finally, security: encrypt endpoints, use strong credentials, and apply strict VPC and security group rules. A common misconception is to deprioritize testing. Key takeaway: plan for conversions, test thoroughly, and size and secure replication infrastructure before production cutover. screens.title: Monitoring, Scaling, and Post-Migration Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring and post-migration work are as important as the migration itself. During migration, monitor replication instance C P U, memory, disk input and output, and replication lag. Use CloudWatch metrics and set alarms for lag thresholds and resource exhaustion. If you observe lag, scale the replication instance or tune table selection and parallelism. After cutover, perform data integrity checks across the full dataset where possible and schedule performance tuning on the target database—indexes, query plans, and connection pooling adjustments. Decommission source systems only after a safe retention period and after confirming backups and audits. Security tasks include rotating credentials, ensuring encryption keys are managed, and updating network ACLs. A common misconception is that cutover ends migration; in reality, the first weeks after cutover require heightened monitoring and performance tuning as workload patterns change. fullNarratorScript:
Database migrations are one of the riskiest parts of cloud moves because databases contain application state and business records. In this lesson you will learn how to choose a migration approach based on whether engines match, how to use AWS Database Migration Service for continuous replication, and when to apply the Schema Conversion Tool or Babelfish to reduce application changes. We will emphasize practical, low-downtime patterns: full initial load plus change data capture, staged cutover steps, and how to validate consistency before switching clients. A short example demonstrates creating DMS endpoints and a replication task from a source database to an Aurora PostgreSQL target. Finally, we will surface common mistakes—type mismatches, incomplete schema conversion, sizing and network issues—and how to mitigate them with testing and monitoring. By the end you will be able to describe a migration plan that balances risk, cost, and business constraints and pick the right AWS tools for homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations.

These learning objectives guide what you should be able to do after completing the chapter. First, you'll identify the practical differences between homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations and decide the right approach for an application. Second, you'll use AWS Database Migration Service to configure endpoints, create a replication instance, and run a full-load plus change data capture task to keep a target database in sync while minimizing downtime. Third, you'll apply AWS Schema Conversion Tool to analyze an existing schema and identify objects that require manual intervention, and you'll understand how to interpret SCT's assessment report. Fourth, you'll design a cutover plan that uses continuous replication, verifies consistency, and safely switches applications to the target. Each objective focuses on demonstrable skills: analyzing migration complexity, configuring DMS, converting schemas with SCT, and planning low-downtime cutovers. These are practical competencies you will verify with hands-on practice and tests.

These additional objectives describe the hands-on and judgment skills you will show. You will be able to apply SCT to generate an assessment report that highlights incompatibilities and required manual refactors. You will create a DMS replication instance and connect endpoints to perform an initial full load and then keep the target synchronized using change data capture, monitoring replication lag and instance health. You will design cutover verification steps, including stopping writes, ensuring the CDC stream is applied, and validating row counts or checksums. Finally, you'll evaluate whether Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL is appropriate to reduce application changes when migrating from S Q L Server. Each objective includes practical acceptance criteria so you can verify success in a staging environment before production cutover. Learning Objectives — Practical outcomes means produce sct reports, run dms tasks with full-load-and-cdc, validate consistency, and evaluate babelfish as a compatibility option.. In practical terms, how you'll demonstrate competence in migration planning and execution. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's define the two primary migration categories and why the distinction drives your plan. A homogeneous migration is when the source and target database engines are the same, for example Oracle to Oracle on RDS. The main complexity there is moving large volumes of data while minimizing downtime; most schema and code constructs remain compatible so the conversion effort is low. A heterogeneous migration is when engines differ, such as S Q L Server to Aurora PostgreSQL. Here the complexity rises because you must translate schemas, stored procedures, and sometimes application S Q L. Converting types, functions, and procedural code is often the most time-consuming work. A concrete example: moving a 500-gigabyte S Q L Server database with many T-S Q L stored procedures to Aurora PostgreSQL will likely require schema conversion, function rewrites, and compatibility testing. A common misconception is that DMS alone solves all heterogeneous issues; in fact DMS handles data movement but not full schema and procedural conversion. Key takeaway: identify the category early to allocate time and tools — native backups or replication for homogeneous moves, plus Schema Conversion Tool and manual refactor work for heterogeneous migrations. What migration type fits your project constraints and resourcing?

AWS Database Migration Service is a managed service that moves data between heterogeneous and homogeneous engines while supporting ongoing replication. At its core DMS uses a replication instance — compute that reads changes from the source and applies them to the target. You configure a source endpoint and a target endpoint, then create a replication task that runs a migration type: full load, CDC, or full-load-and-CDC. The full-load-and-CDC pattern is critical for minimal downtime: DMS performs an initial complete copy and then streams ongoing changes so the target remains synchronized. A concrete example: create a replication instance sized by your workload and start a task that performs full load then CDC. Monitor replication lag, C P U, memory, and input and output; under-sizing the instance leads to lag and delayed cutover. A common misconception is to treat DMS as a one-time copy tool; instead it is intended for continuous replication and supports retries, transformation rules, and table mappings. Key takeaway: use DMS for controlled, monitored data movement and plan replication-instance sizing and network bandwidth to avoid replication bottlenecks. AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) means dms performs the data movement and continuous replication that enables near-zero downtime migrations when combined with proper sizing and monitoring.. In practical terms, what dms does and why it is central to minimal-downtime migrations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding migration types in DMS determines how you achieve your downtime goals. Full load copies existing data from source to target. Change Data Capture captures ongoing changes so you can keep source and target synchronized after the initial copy. The combination full-load-and-CDC is the go-to pattern for minimal downtime: DMS performs an initial full transfer and then streams changes until you are ready to cut over. A concrete example: for a 2 TB database with tight RTO constraints, run full load during an off-peak window, let CDC replicate transactional changes, and plan a short write freeze and verification window before flipping connections. Common misconception: choosing CDC only for an initial migration; CDC-only assumes the target already contains full data. Another operational detail is table mappings and transformation rules — decide which schemas and objects to include to reduce initial load size and speed validation. Key takeaway: pick full-load-and-CDC for minimal downtime and plan table selection, monitoring, and a verification strategy before the cutover. DMS Migration Types and Task Patterns means full-load-and-cdc combines an initial copy with continuous replication to enable near-zero downtime cutovers.. In practical terms, full load, cdc, and full-load-and-cdc explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We'll walk through a conceptual command sequence you can use to provision DMS components. The commands shown are a starting point; in practice you substitute ARNs, network values, and credentials. First, create source and target endpoints with connection strings or server addresses and credentials. Next create a replication instance sized for your workload. Finally, create a replication task that references the endpoints and the instance and chooses full-load-and-CDC. The important idea is that the task performs the initial copy and then streams changes for continuous synchronization. Monitor the task state and replication lag with the console or CloudWatch. A common misconception is to treat the CLI output as the final verification; always validate data consistency with row counts or checksums. Example: after starting the task, validate small sample tables, then perform a full verification. Key takeaway: the CLI is an automation-friendly way to script DMS setup, but validation and monitoring are essential parts of the migration workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A predictable cutover reduces risk. Use these steps to move an application with minimal downtime. Phase one is full load: start DMS full-load to copy existing data. Phase two is CDC: enable continuous replication so changes on the source are applied to the target. Phase three is pre-cutover verification: run row-count and checksum comparisons on sample tables, run application smoke tests against the target in read-only mode if possible, and monitor replication lag until it is negligible. Phase four is the short write freeze: stop writes to the source database, let DMS apply outstanding changes, and verify there are no pending transactions. Phase five is the switch: update application connection strings to the new target and start the application. Phase six is post-cutover monitoring: ensure error logs and performance metrics are healthy and roll back if serious issues appear. A common misconception is skipping verification or trusting row counts alone; include functional smoke tests and data integrity checks. The key takeaway is to script verification and rollback procedures so the cutover is repeatable and testable in staging before production. This screen lists common mistakes teams make during migration and how to avoid them. First, incomplete schema conversion happens when teams assume automated tools fix everything; SCT will flag incompatibilities but manual refactor for stored procedures and proprietary functions is often required. Second, data type mismatches can silently corrupt data if types are mapped incorrectly; always test edge cases and validate conversion logic. Third, network latency between source, replication instance, and target can slow replication and increase lag; for large migrations consider Direct Connect or replication instances in the same region and subnet placement. Fourth, under-sizing the replication instance leads to C P U or input and output bottlenecks and replication lag; monitor metrics and scale instances proactively. Fifth, transaction log retention must be configured so CDC can read changes; short retention causes missed changes. Finally, security: encrypt endpoints, use strong credentials, and apply strict VPC and security group rules. A common misconception is to deprioritize testing. Key takeaway: plan for conversions, test thoroughly, and size and secure replication infrastructure before production cutover.
